data.title: Targeting HER2 by Combination Therapies
data.journal: Journal of clinical oncology : official journal of the American Society of Clinical Oncology
data.fulltext:
HER2 was initially recognized 30 years ago as an amplified oncogene in more than 20% of breast cancers, and following the genomic revolution of the more recent decade, is now known to be amplified in subsets of many other types of cancer. Since the earliest days of its discovery, attempts to treat cancers harboring amplification and overexpression of HER2 have been ongoing with five such drugs on the market and a multitude of others in the investigational pipelines. A similar paradigm for the treatment of cancers driven by other oncogenes such as EGFR and Alk in lung cancers, BRAF in melanomas, Bcr-Abl in CML, Kit in gastrointestinal stromal tumors and others followed these developments with HER2. While the treatment of these cancers with inhibitors of their oncogenes has led to highly effective monotherapy standards entirely eliminating chemotherapy components, the treatment of HER2-amplified cancers has followed a different path focusing on combinations of HER2-targeting agents and often as components of larger regimens involving chemo or hormonal therapies. One such triple combination is reported by Johnston et al in this issue of JCO. The key distinction that has set HER2 along a different course from these other oncogenes is that HER2 is activated through gene amplification and massive overexpression whereas the others are activated through structural alteration or fusion events. An important lesson of history has been that the amplified oncogene is a considerably more difficult target for pharmaceutical inactivation than the mutated oncogene, thus necessitating cocktails of HER2-targeting drugs that even in combinations, still can’t mimick the monotherapy activities of EGFR or Alk inhibitors in lung cancers.

HER2 is a receptor tyrosine kinase that spans the surface membrane of cells. The extracellular half does not itself bind ligands, but is designed to recognize ligand-activated forms of its family members EGFR, HER3, or HER4 leading to dimerization with these receptor partners. The cytoplasmic part of HER2 and its partners contain a catalytic kinase domain and the dimerization event leads to a kinase domain interaction that unleashes HER2 kinase activity (Figure 1). The end result is phosphorylation of the long cytoplasmic tail on various tyrosine residues and the recruitment of second messenger proteins to these phosphotyrosines. When the gene is amplified in cancer cells, the result is massive overexpression of HER2, and constitutive dimerization and signaling events that are not solicited through the physiologic ligand-stimulation mechanism, and the unrelenting activation of numerous downstream biologic pathways that promote the malignant phenotype.

Efforts to develop drugs targeting HER2 have explored a diverse mechanistic landscape. The monoclonal antibody class of therapeutics are large molecules that can bind extracellular epitopes such as the extracellular region of HER2 on the surface of cells. Trastuzumab is a monoclonal antibody that was developed in the era before our understanding of HER2 structure, but is now recognized to bind at an epitope just outside the surface membrane. Monoclonal antibodies can be mechanistically complex agents. They can be used as inhibitors, to disrupt the function of the target they bind. But antibodies are also immunologic effectors and their binding to tumor cells can initiate or enhance an anti-tumor immune response. In the early days of the field, the binding of trastuzumab was felt to somehow interfere with the signaling function of HER2, but extensive evidence spanning the subsequent decades has failed to confirm such a mechanism of action. However a plethora of studies now supports an immunologic mode of action of trastuzumab. This has now spawned a variety of efforts to enhance this activity through antibody engineering or using regimens that combine trastuzumab with checkpoint inhibitors and other immune enhancers. The monoclonal antibody pertuzumab was developed with structural specificity in mind and binds a site on HER2 where it could interfere with dimerization and thus rationally disrupt signaling function. This design concept does work when HER2 levels are low, but is overpowered when HER2 is massively overexpressed and ineffective at inhibiting HER2 signaling in these HER2-amplified cancer cells. The clinical benefits observed with pertuzumab remain to be mechanistically defined and may also be immunologically mediated. Since the activities of trastuzumab and pertuzumab are modest as monotherapy or dual therapy, their clinical use has been predominantly in combinations with other HER2-targeting or chemotherapeutic or hormonal agents.

The mechanistic functions effected by antibodies has extended well beyond the disruption of target function or the recruitment of immunologic effectors. Due to advances in protein engineering within the pharmaceutical industry, antibodies can now be engineered to function as carriers to deliver reagents to cancer cells. This requires that the target be relatively specific to cancer cells and the massive surface expression of HER2 provides such a degree of specificity. HER2-targeting antibodies have been used successfully to target imaging molecules, radioisotopes, anti-cancer drugs, liposomes, and nanoparticles to HER2-amplified tumors. Ado-trastuzumab emtansine, the toxin-linked version of trastuzumab, delivers a potent microtubule toxin and is now widely used in the treatment of HER2-amplified breast cancer and other such antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) are under development.

The mechanistic intent to inactivate HER2 signaling was brought closer to fruition by the development of small molecule inhibitors of its catalytic function. Drugs such as lapatinib and neratinib bind in the active site of the intracellular kinase domain and inhibit catalysis that is essential for phosphorylation and signaling. The structural features of lapatinib enable it to bind the HER2 kinase domain with remarkable selectivity while the chemical features of neratinib generate a covalent bond with HER2 that allows it to bind irreversibly. Although the inactivation of the kinase domain provides a solid mechanistic rationale for inhibiting HER2 signaling function, the massive amount of HER2 has yet again proven too high for complete inactivation, accounting for the modest clinical activities of these kinase inhibitors. Any degree of inhibition short of complete inactivation leads to compensatory increases in its partner HER3 and sufficient HER2-HER3 signaling to drive tumor growth. Due to its modest activities as monotherapy, the clinical use of lapatinib has been entirely directed towards combinations with other HER2-targeting or chemotherapeutic agents. The clinical use of neratinib continues to be explored with benefits demonstrated in the extended adjuvant therapy setting and its tolerability in various combination therapy approaches being established.

The observed difficulties in inactivating the massive amount of HER2 on cancer cells with any one drug underlies the modest activities of individual drugs, but has motivated the development of combinations of HER2-targeting drugs. In particular, the antibody class and small molecule kinase inhibitor class have different toxicity profiles making them suitable for combination approaches. Although the term “dual blockade” is occasionally used in reference to such combinations targeting the extracellular and intracellular regions of HER2, the term is more imagery than functional description as the mode of action of such combinations likely involves the dual mechanisms of partial function blockade and immunologic recruitment rather than dual types of blockade.

A significant body of work from cell-based and mouse genetic studies have highlighted the important role of HER3 as an essential partner for HER2 in HER2-amplified cancers and a harbinger of resistance to HER2-targeting agents. This has focused attention on HER3 as a potential collateral target for combination therapy approaches. However from a pharmaceutical perspective, inactivating HER3 function in these cancers has proven particularly challenging. Antibodies binding the extracellular region of HER3 can indeed interfere with the ligand binding and activation of HER3 and its dimerization with HER2, similar in design concept to the development of the HER2 antibody pertuzumab. But this approach again falls short when HER2 is massively overexpressed such as in these cancer cells, likely because of the unconventional and overpowering ways, not well understood, by which massively overexpressed HER2 engages HER3. The intracellular kinase domain of HER3 lacks catalytic activity and small molecule inhibitors that bind the kinase domain of HER3, analogous to lapatinib or neratinib for HER2, have no effects on its signaling functions. Other innovative approaches are being pursued to develop inhibitors of HER3 for use in combinations with HER2-targeting drugs.

Thus continues efforts to tackle one of the earliest oncogenes to be identified in human cancers. Although the inactivation of HER2 has proven challenging, it has provided a diverse mechanistic landscape and a multitude of targeting approaches that have contributed to fruitful combination therapy approaches. The investigational pipelines are rich with yet more approaches and the cocktails of HER2-targeting therapies are only going to get bigger.
